newsitem.title: CHILE: Chilean salmon raisers may be sued in U.S. - report.
newsitem.headline: Chilean salmon raisers may be sued in U.S. - report.

text.p: Chilean salmon producers are expecting U.S. producers to sue them on charges of illegally dumping salmon in the American market, a Chilean newspaper reported on Sunday.

If proved, the charge could lead to trade sanctions costing Chilean exporters more than the $200 million they say they lost in a five-day ban on Chilean fruit in the United States in 1989 after two Chilean grapes were found tainted with cyanide, said the daily El Mercurio.

Chilean producers, who exported about $180 million worth of farmed salmon to the United States last year, are expecting their U.S. counterparts to file the charges with the Commerce Department imminently, said the report.
To prove dumping charges, the accuser must generally show that the producer is selling below cost, or below the cost at which it sells the product in its home market.

The charges could open a major new trade dispute between the United States and Chile at a time when officials in Santiago have been hoping to resume talks to join the North American Free Trade Agreement, or NAFTA, after the November elections.
Chilean officials, including Foreign Minister Jose Miguel Insulza and the lower house of Congress' Economy Committee, met recently to discuss the potential salmon dispute, El Mercurio reported.
The dumping charge is expected to mention 15 specific Chilean producers, although any trade sanctions would likely affect the whole Chilean salmon industry, said the report.

In the past 15 years, Chile has become a major producer of farmed salmon. Output has gone from virutally zero in the late 1970s to about 100,000 tonnes last year, making it the world's second largest producer of farmed salmon after Norway.
Local salmon raisers admit Chile's booming production has contributed to a sharp drop in supermarket salmon prices around the world.
